intro: Say your name out loud. Say it slowly. Can you hear the pieces? Every word you say is made of small sounds. Your ears can find them. Your mouth can say them one at a time. That is where reading starts.

Letters are a code for those sounds. The letter m stands for /m/. Put letters in a row and they spell a word. Learn the code and the letters tell you what to say. Cat. Ship. Cape. Words you can read all by yourself.

In this unit you will hear the first sound, the last sound and the middle sound. You will rhyme and clap. You will blend sounds into words and take words apart. Then you will learn the letters, the vowels, the letter teams and the silent e. By the end, you will crack the code.
bigQuestion: How do the sounds you hear become words you can read?

timeline.t: Say a word slowly and hear the sounds inside it
Find the first sound: /b/ for ball, /d/ for dog
Find the last sound and the middle sound
Rhyme: cat, hat, bat. The ends match
Blend /s/ /u/ /n/ into sun, then take it apart
Change one sound: pin, pan, man
Learn that each letter has a name and a sound
Meet the five vowels and their short sounds
Read the letter teams sh, ch and th
Add a silent e: cap becomes cape
Read a whole line, left to right, all by yourself

words.d: one small piece of a word that you hear
when two words end with the same sound, like cat and hat
one beat in a word; apple has two
saying sounds together fast so they make a word
the big form of a letter, like B
one of the letters a, e, i, o, u
two letters that make one sound together, like sh
an e at the end of a word that makes no sound but changes the vowel

test.q: How many sounds are in the word sun?
test.why: Say it slowly: s... u... n. That is three sounds.

test.q: What is the first sound in fish?
test.why: The sound at the very start of fish is /f/.
Bed and red both end with -ed. Their ends sound the same.

test.q: How many claps does elephant get?
test.why: El-e-phant. Three beats, so three claps.
Say the sounds fast and close together. They make map.

test.q: Change the /c/ in cat to /b/. What word do you get?
test.why: Take off /c/ and put on /b/. C-at becomes b-at.

test.q: When you read a word, what do you use?
test.why: You read with sounds. Map is /m/ /a/ /p/, not em-ay-pee.

test.q: Which word has a vowel in the middle that says its short sound?
test.why: Pig is consonant, vowel, consonant. The i says /i/.

test.q: What sound do c and h make together in chip?
test.why: C and h are a team. Together they say /ch/.

test.q: What does the silent e do in cape?
choices: Makes the a say its name
test.why: The e is silent. It tells the a to say its name, ay.

write.prompt: Pick one word you can read now, like ship or cape. Tell how you read it. Say what sounds you hear, what letters you see, and how you put them together.
tips: Start with your word. Write it big.
Say the sounds you hear, first to last.
Tell about any letter team or silent e.
Say how you blended the sounds into the word.
Draw a picture of your word.

title: Sounds and Letters

chapters.title: Sounds in Words
chapters.bigQuestion: What do you hear inside a word?

story.title: I Spy With My Ears
story.kicker: The clue is not a color. The clue is a sound.
paragraphs: It is rug time in Ms. Ortiz's class. She says, "Let's play I Spy. But today the clue is a sound." The kids lean in. Ms. Ortiz says, "I spy something that starts with /b/." She says the sound, not the letter. Just /b/, like a bubble popping.

Hands go up. "Ball!" says Devon. Ms. Ortiz shakes her head. "Good try. Ball does start with /b/. But I do not see a ball." Kids look around the room. There is a clock. There is a door. There is a book.

Priya says the word slowly. "Buh... book. Book starts with /b/!" Ms. Ortiz smiles. "Yes! The first sound in book is /b/." Now it is Priya's turn. She looks around. She says, "I spy something that starts with /d/."
Devon says, "Door!" He is right. Every word in the room has a first sound. Clock. Rug. Window. Once you hear the first sound, you can play this game anywhere.
story.think: Look around your room. Pick one thing. What sound does its name start with?

lessons.title: Words Are Made of Sounds
lessons.mainIdea: Every word is made of small sounds put together.
reading: Say the word cat. Now say it very slowly. Stretch it out. Do you hear it? C... a... t. Cat is not one sound. Cat is three sounds. They are stuck together.
Every word is like this. A *word* is a set of *sounds* said in a row. Say sun slowly. S... u... n. Three sounds. Say go slowly. G... o. Two sounds.
Your ears can pull a word apart. Your mouth can say each piece. This is a big skill. When you hear the sounds, you are ready to read them.

words.d: a set of sounds said together that means something
one small piece of a word that you hear

look.title: How Many Sounds?
look.prompt: Say jump slowly. Can you hear all four sounds?

check.q: How many sounds are in the word cat?
check.why: Say it slowly: c... a... t. That is three sounds stuck together.

check.q: What is a word made of?
check.why: A word is a set of sounds said together. Cat has three of them.

check.q: How can you hear the sounds in a word?
check.why: When you say a word slowly, you can hear each piece.

lessons.title: The First Sound
lessons.mainIdea: The first sound is the sound you hear at the start of a word.
reading: Say mom. What sound comes out first? /m/. Your lips press together. That is the *first sound*. Now say dog. The first sound is /d/. Your tongue taps the top of your mouth.
The first sound is the start of the word. It is the sound you hear before all the others. Say sun. /s/ comes first. Say fish. /f/ comes first.
Play a game. Say your name slowly. What sound comes first? Now say a friend's name. Do they start the same? Maria and Max both start with /m/.

words.d: the sound at the very start of a word

look.title: Two Bags of Toys
look.text: Look at two bags. One bag is for /b/ things. One bag is for /s/ things. Here are the toys: a ball, a sock, a bear, a spoon, a boat. Say each one slowly. Listen for the first sound. Then drop it in the right bag.
look.prompt: Which toys go in the /b/ bag? How do you know?

check.q: What is the first sound in dog?
check.why: Say dog slowly. The sound at the very start is /d/.

check.q: Which word starts with /s/?
check.why: Sock starts with /s/. Bear starts with /b/. Fish starts with /f/.

check.q: Where do you hear the first sound?
choices: At the end of a word
In the middle of a word
At the start of a word
check.why: The first sound is the very start. In mom, it is /m/.

lessons.title: Last Sound, Middle Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Words have a last sound and a middle sound too.
reading: Say bus. Say it slowly. B... u... s. The *last sound* is /s/. It is the sound at the end. Say cup. The last sound is /p/. Your lips pop.
Now find the *middle sound*. Say cat slowly. C... a... t. The middle sound is /a/. It sits between /c/ and /t/. Say pig. The middle sound is /i/.
The middle sound is the hard one. It is short. It goes by fast. So stretch the word out. Say it like a slow song. Caaaat. Now you can hear the /a/.

words.d: the sound at the very end of a word
the sound between the first sound and the last sound

look.title: Cat, Cot, Cut
look.text: Say these three words slowly. Cat. Cot. Cut. They all start with /c/. They all end with /t/. But they are not the same word. Listen to the middle. Cat has /a/. Cot has /o/. Cut has /u/. The middle sound changes everything.
look.prompt: Which sound is different in cat, cot and cut?

check.q: What is the last sound in bus?
check.why: Say bus slowly. The sound at the end is /s/.

check.q: What is the middle sound in cat?
check.why: C... a... t. The /a/ sits in the middle.

check.q: Why is the middle sound hard to hear?
check.why: The middle sound is short. Stretching the word helps you hear it.

lessons.title: Words That Rhyme
lessons.mainIdea: Words rhyme when their ends sound the same.
reading: Say cat. Say hat. Listen to the ends. C-at. H-at. Both end with -at. Cat and hat *rhyme*. Two words rhyme when their ends sound the same.
Try more. Dog and log. Sun and fun. Bed and red. The first sound is different. The rest of the word matches. That is why they sound like a pair.
Rhymes are all over songs and poems. Twinkle, twinkle, little star. How I wonder what you are. Star and are rhyme. Your ears already know this game.

words.d: when two words end with the same sound, like cat and hat

look.title: A Rhyme You Can Say
look.text: Ten little ducks sat in the sun. One little duck went off to run. Nine little ducks said, "That was fun!"
look.prompt: Which three words rhyme? Say them out loud.

check.q: Which word rhymes with cat?
check.why: Cat and hat both end with -at. Their ends sound the same.

check.q: When do two words rhyme?
choices: When their ends sound the same
check.why: Rhymes match at the end. Sun and fun both end with -un.

check.q: Sun and fun rhyme. Which part is different?
check.why: Sun starts with /s/. Fun starts with /f/. The rest is the same.

lessons.title: Clap the Parts
lessons.mainIdea: You can clap the beats in a word to count its parts.
reading: Say apple. Clap as you say it. Ap-ple. Two claps. Now say cat. One clap. Say banana. Ba-na-na. Three claps. Each clap is one *syllable*. A syllable is one beat of a word.
Try your name. Say it and clap. Sam gets one clap. Ma-ri-a gets three claps. Long names get more claps. Short names get one.
Put your hand under your chin. Say elephant. El-e-phant. Your chin drops three times. That is three syllables. Your chin can count for you.

words.d: one beat in a word; apple has two

look.title: Clap and Count
look.prompt: Which food name has the most beats? Clap it out.

check.q: How many claps does apple get?
check.why: Ap-ple. Two beats, so two claps.

check.q: What is a syllable?
choices: The first sound of a word
check.why: A syllable is one beat. Banana has three beats.

check.q: Your chin drops three times when you say a word. How many syllables is that?
check.why: Your chin drops once for each beat. Three drops means three syllables.

lessons.title: Blend the Sounds
lessons.mainIdea: Put sounds together in a row and they make a word.
reading: Listen. /m/... /a/... /p/. Three sounds, one at a time. Now say them fast. Push them together. Map! You just made a word. This is called *blending*.
Blending is like gluing beads on a string. Each sound is a bead. Say them close together. /s/ /u/ /n/. Sun. /d/ /o/ /g/. Dog.
Go slow at first. Say the first sound. Hold it. Slide into the next one. Sssuuunnn. Then say it fast. Sun. Readers do this all day long.

words.d: saying sounds together fast so they make a word

look.title: The Robot Talks
look.text: A toy robot says words in pieces. It says, "/p/... /i/... /g/." Its friend Lena hears the sounds. She pushes them together in her head. She says, "Pig!" The robot beeps. It says, "/h/... /a/... /t/." Lena smiles. She knows this one too.
look.prompt: What word did the robot say the second time?

check.q: What is blending?
choices: Putting sounds together to make a word
Clapping the beats of a word
check.why: Blending pushes sounds together. /m/ /a/ /p/ becomes map.

check.q: Blend these sounds: /s/ /u/ /n/. What word is it?
check.why: Say the sounds fast and close. They make the word sun.

check.q: What should you do when blending is hard?
choices: Go slow and hold each sound
check.why: Slow blending works. Hold the first sound and slide to the next.

lessons.title: Take a Word Apart
lessons.mainIdea: You can break a word into its sounds, one at a time.
reading: Blending puts sounds together. Now go the other way. Say the word hop. Pull it apart. /h/... /o/... /p/. You broke hop into three sounds. That is *taking apart*.
Use your fingers. Say sit. Hold up one finger for each sound. /s/ is one. /i/ is two. /t/ is three. Three fingers. Three sounds.
This helps you spell. To write a word, you need its sounds. Say the word. Take it apart. Then write one letter for each sound you hear.

words.d: saying each sound in a word one at a time

look.title: Fingers Up
look.text: Jamal wants to write the word bug. He says it slowly. He puts up one finger. /b/. Two fingers. /u/. Three fingers. /g/. Now he has three fingers up. He knows bug has three sounds. He can write one letter for each one.
look.prompt: Why does Jamal hold up his fingers?

check.q: Take apart the word hop. What are the sounds?
check.why: Hop has three sounds in this order: /h/, /o/, /p/.

check.q: How many fingers do you hold up for sit?
check.why: Sit has three sounds: /s/, /i/, /t/. One finger for each.

check.q: How does taking a word apart help you?
choices: It helps you spell the word
check.why: When you hear each sound, you can write a letter for each one.

lessons.title: Change One Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Change one sound in a word and you get a new word.
reading: Say cat. Now take off the /c/. Put /h/ in its place. Hat! Take off the /h/. Put on /b/. Bat! You changed one sound. You made a new word each time.
You can change the end too. Say cat. Take off the /t/. Put on /p/. Cap! You can change the middle. Cat. Cot. Cut. One small change makes a whole new word.
This is a *word game* you can play anywhere. Start with pin. Change one sound. Pan. Change one more. Man. Keep going. How far can you get?

words.d: a game where you play with the sounds in words

look.title: The Word Ladder
look.text: Look at the word ladder. On the first step is the word cat. Change one sound. Step up to hat. Change one sound. Step up to hot. Change one sound. Step up to pot. Each step is a new word. Each step is only one sound away from the last one.
look.prompt: Which sound changed to go from hat to hot?

check.q: Change the /c/ in cat to /h/. What word do you get?
check.why: Take off /c/ and put on /h/. C-at becomes h-at, hat.

check.q: Cat becomes cap. Which sound changed?
check.why: The /t/ at the end became /p/. The first and middle sounds stayed.

check.q: What happens when you change one sound in a word?
check.why: One sound change makes a new word. Pin becomes pan.

review.q: What is a word made of?
review.why: Every word is a set of sounds put together. Cat has three.

review.q: What is the first sound in sun?
review.why: Say sun slowly. The sound at the very start is /s/.
Dog and log both end with -og. Their ends sound the same.

review.q: How many claps does banana get?
review.why: Ba-na-na. Three beats, so three claps.
Say the sounds fast and close together. They make dog.

review.q: Change the /p/ in pin to /f/. What word do you get?
review.why: Take off /p/ and put on /f/. P-in becomes f-in.

chapters.title: Letters and the Code
chapters.bigQuestion: How do letters turn sounds into words you can read?

story.title: Cracking the Code on Ship
story.kicker: Four letters. Three sounds. One class that would not give up.
paragraphs: Mr. Bell writes a word on the board. S-h-i-p. "Who can read this?" he asks. Nobody says a thing. The class knows /s/. They know /h/. But together the letters make a strange word. Suh-hip? That is not a word.
Then Ava says, "Wait. What if s and h are a team?" Mr. Bell nods. He puts his finger to his lips. "Shhh." The class laughs. That is the sound! Two letters, one sound. /sh/.
Now they try again. Ava points to each letter, left to right. /sh/... /i/... /p/. She says it faster. Ship! The whole class says it. Ship! A boat on the lake. They just cracked the code.
Mr. Bell writes more words. Shop. Fish. Dish. Now the class can read them all. Once you know the code, the letters tell you what to say.
story.think: What made ship hard to read at first? What made it easy at the end?

lessons.title: A Name and a Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Every letter has a name and a sound, and the sound is what you read.
reading: Look at the letter m. Its *name* is em. But when you read, you do not say em. You say its *sound*: /m/. Say it. Your lips press together. Mmm. That is the sound of m.
Every letter has both. The letter s is called ess. Its sound is /s/, like a snake. The letter t is called tee. Its sound is /t/, a quick tap.
The name helps you talk about the letter. The sound helps you read the word. Map is not em-ay-pee. Map is /m/ /a/ /p/. Sounds make words.

words.d: what a letter is called, like em for the letter m
what a letter says in a word, like /m/ for the letter m

look.title: Two Ways to Say It
look.text: Look at a box of cereal. On the front is one big letter: S. Ben says, "That is an ess." His sister says, "It says /s/." They are both right. Ess is the name. /s/ is the sound. When Ben reads the word sun, he does not say ess. He says /s/.
look.prompt: When you read a word, do you use the letter's name or its sound?

check.q: What is the sound of the letter m?
check.why: The name is em. The sound is /m/, with your lips pressed together.

check.q: Which one helps you read a word?
check.why: You read with sounds. Map is /m/ /a/ /p/, not em-ay-pee.

check.q: What is the letter s called?
check.why: The name of the letter s is ess. Its sound is /s/.

lessons.title: Big Letters, Small Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Each letter comes in a capital and a small form, and both say the same sound.
reading: Look at B and b. They look different. One is big. One is small. But they are the same letter. Both are bee. Both say /b/. The big one is a *capital* letter. The small one is a *lowercase* letter.
Capitals do a special job. A name starts with a capital. Maria. Chicago. The first word in a sentence starts with a capital too. The dog ran.
Most letters in a book are small. Capitals show up at the start of things. Look at your name. The first letter is a capital. The rest are small.

words.d: the big form of a letter, like B
the small form of a letter, like b

look.title: Matching Socks
look.text: Look at a pile of letter cards. Some are big. Some are small. Your job is to match them like socks. A goes with a. G goes with g. Some pairs look alike, like S and s. Some pairs look very different, like A and a. But every pair says the same sound.
look.prompt: Which pairs look alike? Which pairs look different?

check.q: What is the big form of a letter called?
check.why: The big form is the capital. B is a capital. b is lowercase.

check.q: Do B and b say the same sound?
choices: Only the big one says a sound
check.why: B and b are the same letter in two forms. Both say /b/.

check.q: Where do you see a capital letter?
choices: In the middle of every word
At the end of a word
At the start of a name
check.why: Names start with a capital. So does the first word of a sentence.

lessons.title: Vowels and Consonants
lessons.mainIdea: Five letters are vowels, and every word needs at least one.
reading: Say /a/. Your mouth is open. Air comes out with nothing in the way. Now say /t/. Your tongue taps. Something blocks the air. Open sounds are *vowels*. Blocked sounds are *consonants*.
The vowel letters are a, e, i, o and u. Just five. All the other letters are consonants. B, c, d, f, g and more.
Every word needs a vowel. Look at cat. The vowel is a. Look at dog. The vowel is o. Try to say a word with no vowel. Bkt? It is not a word. The vowel holds the word together.

words.d: one of the letters a, e, i, o, u; its sound comes out with an open mouth
any letter that is not a vowel, like b, s or t

look.title: Five Vowels, Many Consonants
look.prompt: Are there more vowels or more consonants?

check.q: Which letters are vowels?
check.why: The five vowels are a, e, i, o and u. The rest are consonants.

check.q: What is the vowel in dog?
check.why: The letter o is a vowel. D and g are consonants.

check.q: How is a vowel sound made?
check.why: A vowel sound comes out with nothing in the way. Say /a/ and feel it.

lessons.title: Short Vowels
lessons.mainIdea: In a short word like cat, the vowel says its short sound.
reading: Look at the word cat. The vowel is a. Here it says /a/, like the start of apple. This is the *short sound* of a. Say cat, hat, bat, map. Every one has short a.
Each vowel has a short sound. E says /e/ in bed. I says /i/ in pig. O says /o/ in hot. U says /u/ in cup. Learn these five and you can read hundreds of words.
Here is the rule. A word with one vowel in the middle usually says the short sound. Cat. Bed. Pig. Hot. Cup. Consonant, vowel, consonant. Say the sounds and blend.

words.d: the sound a vowel makes in a short word, like /a/ in cat

look.title: Five Short Words
look.text: The cat sat on the mat. The pig is big. The hen is in the pen. The dog got hot. The pup is in the tub.
look.prompt: Find the vowel in each short word. Which sound does it make?

check.q: What sound does a make in cat?
check.why: In a short word like cat, the vowel a says its short sound, /a/.

check.q: Which word has short i?
check.why: Pig has the vowel i in the middle. It says /i/.

check.q: A word has one vowel in the middle, like hot. What sound does the vowel say?
check.why: Consonant, vowel, consonant words usually use the short vowel sound.

lessons.title: Two Letters, One Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Some letter pairs, like sh, ch and th, make one new sound together.
reading: Look at ship. Four letters. But only three sounds. The letters s and h work as a *team*. Together they say /sh/. Put your finger to your lips. Shhh. That is the sound.
Other teams do this too. C and h say /ch/, like in chip. Say it. Your tongue clicks. T and h say /th/, like in thin. Your tongue pokes out a little.
When you see sh, ch or th, do not say each letter. Say the team sound. Fish. Chop. Bath. Look for the teams, and the words get easier.

words.d: two letters that make one sound together, like sh

look.title: Letters and Sounds
look.prompt: Ship has four letters. Why does it have only three sounds?

check.q: What sound do s and h make together?
check.why: S and h are a team. Together they say /sh/, like in ship.

check.q: Which word has the /ch/ sound?
check.why: Chip starts with the team c and h. They say /ch/.

check.q: Ship has four letters. How many sounds does it have?
check.why: Sh is one sound. Then /i/ and /p/. That makes three.

lessons.title: The Silent e
lessons.mainIdea: An e at the end of a word makes the vowel say its name.
reading: Look at cap. Short a. /cap/. Now add an e to the end. Cape. The a changed! Now it says its name, ay. And the e says nothing at all. It is a *silent e*.
The silent e is a helper. It sits at the end. It makes no sound. But it tells the vowel to say its name. Kit becomes kite. Hop becomes hope. Cub becomes cube.
Watch for the e at the end. Cover it with your finger. Read the short word. Then let the e back in. Say the vowel's name. Pin. Pine. You can hear the change.

words.d: an e at the end of a word that makes no sound but changes the vowel

look.title: The Magic Finger
look.text: Look at the word kite on the board. Maya covers the e with her finger. Now she sees kit. She reads it: kit. She lifts her finger. The e is back. Now the i says its name. She reads it again: kite. One little letter turned a small box into a thing that flies.
look.prompt: What did the silent e change in the word kite?

check.q: What does a silent e do?
choices: Makes the vowel say its name
check.why: The e is silent. It tells the vowel before it to say its name.

check.q: Add a silent e to cap. What word do you get?
check.why: Cap plus e is cape. Now the a says its name, ay.

check.q: What sound does the e make in kite?
check.why: The e at the end is silent. It makes no sound of its own.

lessons.title: Read Left to Right
lessons.mainIdea: Read the letters in order from left to right, and you get the right word.
reading: Look at the word pat. Point to the p. That is the *left* side. Now slide your finger to the right. P... a... t. Pat. You read the letters in order.
Order matters. The letters t, a and p can spell tap. Or pat. Or apt. Same letters, different words. Start on the left. Go to the right. Then you get the right word.
Lines work the same way. Read a line from left to right. When you reach the end, jump down. Start again on the left. Your finger can lead the way.

words.d: the side where you start reading

look.title: Same Letters, Two Words
look.text: Look at three letter cards on a table: t, o, p. Read them left to right. Top. Now flip the order: p, o, t. Read left to right again. Pot. A top spins. A pot holds soup. Same three letters, but a different word each time.
look.prompt: Why is top a different word from pot?

check.q: Which side do you start reading on?
check.why: Reading starts on the left and moves to the right.

check.q: Read these letters in order: p, a, t. What word is it?
check.why: Left to right, the sounds are /p/ /a/ /t/. That is pat.

check.q: What happens when you reach the end of a line?
choices: You jump down and start on the left
check.why: Each new line starts on the left again. Your finger can lead the way.

lessons.title: Write the Letters in Order
lessons.mainIdea: The alphabet has 26 letters in a set order, and you can write each one.
reading: Start at the top. Pull down. Lift. Cross. That is a t. Every letter has a way to be made. Start at the top for most letters. Sit the letter on the line. Make small letters small.
All the letters together are the *alphabet*. There are 26. They go in an order. A, b, c, d, e, f, g. The order never changes. The song you know puts them in a row.
The order is useful. Names on a list go in alphabet order. Books on a shelf go that way too. Write a, b and c on a paper. Then keep going. Can you get all the way to z?

words.d: all 26 letters in their set order, from a to z

look.title: Letters in the Alphabet
look.prompt: How many letters come after j in the alphabet?

check.q: How many letters are in the alphabet?
check.why: The alphabet has 26 letters, from a to z.

check.q: Which letter comes right after b?
check.why: The order is a, b, c. So c comes right after b.

check.q: Where do you start when you write most letters?
check.why: Start at the top and pull down. That is how most letters are made.

review.q: What is the sound of the letter s?
review.why: Ess is the name. /s/ is the sound you use to read.
The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. B and t are consonants.

review.q: What sound do s and h make together?
review.why: S and h are a team. Together they say /sh/, like in ship.

review.q: Add a silent e to hop. What word do you get?
review.why: Hop plus e is hope. The o now says its name.

review.q: Which word has a short a sound?
review.why: Cat has one vowel in the middle. The a says /a/.

review.q: Which way do you read a word?
review.why: Start on the left and move to the right. That gives the right word.
